answer.label: Not Socrates — a 1920s coinage
answer.authorName: Unknown — earliest documented in Wallace Rice (1927)
answer.authorDates: Exact phrasing first documented 1927–28 · falsely pinned on Socrates (c. 469–399 BC)
answer.sourceLine: Widely pinned on Socrates — and also on Oscar Wilde, Voltaire, Mark Twain and Benjamin Franklin — but Quote Investigator found no substantive support for any of them. The self-cancelling twist first surfaces in the 1920s: in Wallace Rice’s Pagan Pictures (1927) and in English newspapers of 1927–28, more than two thousand years after Socrates.

source.excerpt: Nothing too much, doth Chilo say? / Be moderate despite temptation? / Aye; moderate in every way / Be moderate in moderation.
trail: Quote Investigator examined this exact saying and found “no substantive support” for crediting it to Socrates, Oscar Wilde, Voltaire, Mark Twain or Benjamin Franklin.
The earliest documented English match is a quatrain in Wallace Rice’s Pagan Pictures (1927), a free expansion of the Greek Anthology; the familiar wording appears in newspapers of 1927–28.
The underlying thought — “nothing too much” — is the ancient Delphic maxim (echoed by Hesiod and Plautus), not a line traceable to Socrates in particular.
It does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s Socrates page — not even in its Misattributed section.
source.excerptNote: Wallace Rice’s 1927 quatrain “Moderation” is the earliest documented English match. The now-standard wording — “Be moderate in everything, including moderation” — appears in the same 1927–28 window (The Daily Mail of Hull, Dec 1927; the Yale Record, 1928), with no named author.
source.rightsNote: The self-cancelling twist “including moderation” is an anonymous saying with no identifiable author. Its earliest documented print appearances — Wallace Rice’s Pagan Pictures and English newspapers of 1927–28 — are pre-1931 and would themselves be public domain, but no single work or author can be said to own this exact wording, so no status is asserted.

author.name: Wallace Rice
author.heading: The poet, not the philosopher
author.metaLine: 1859–1939 · American poet, editor & translator; designer of the Chicago flag
author.bio: Wallace deGroot Cecil Rice (1859–1939) was a Chicago writer, editor and translator who produced more than ninety books and, in 1917, designed the municipal flag of Chicago. His 1927 collection Pagan Pictures freely reworked the Greek Anthology; its poem “Moderation” is the earliest documented English source of the ‘moderate in moderation’ conceit. Whether Rice coined the exact popular wording or merely versified a quip already circulating is unresolved — but it plainly is not Socrates.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: A feel-good paradox that gets attached to whichever wise name is handy. Quote Investigator ran down the usual suspects and cleared them all.

items.why: The most common modern credit, but no dialogue or ancient testimonium contains it, and Quote Investigator found no substantive support. It is absent even from Wikiquote’s Socrates page.
Widely circulated in the form “Everything in moderation, including moderation” and pinned on Wilde on Goodreads and elsewhere, but it appears in none of his works and is unsupported.
All three are floated as authors, and all three are dismissed for lack of evidence in Quote Investigator’s survey.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented English appearances date to 1927–28 — a 20th-century witticism riffing on the ancient Delphic maxim “nothing too much,” not a line from Socrates, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Ancient idea, modern joke
lead: The sentiment is genuinely ancient. “Nothing too much” (μηδεν αγαν) was one of the maxims inscribed at Delphi, and the value of moderation echoes through Hesiod and the Roman playwright Plautus. None of that, however, contains the self-cancelling punchline that makes the modern line memorable.

That twist — be moderate even about moderation — surfaces only in the 1920s: Wallace Rice’s 1927 quatrain and English newspapers of 1927–28. Quote-collectors later back-dated it onto Socrates, Wilde and others to lend a bit of borrowed gravitas.
